examples.label: aⁿbⁿ
examples.purpose: Recursion with a cheap guess: each failed alternative is undone at once, and nothing deeper has to be revisited.

examples.label: Wrong first guess
examples.purpose: A takes one a, the b then fails, and the parser must go back into A for its second way. The jump back is the point.

examples.label: Palindromes
examples.purpose: Guessing the middle: no amount of lookahead tells where a palindrome turns, so the parser has to try the possibilities.
text: S -> a S a | b S b | a | b | eps

examples.label: Dangling else
examples.purpose: The longer alternative goes first, so an else binds to the nearest if; the shared prefix is matched again when it fails.
text: S -> if c then S else S | if c then S | x
strings: if c then if c then x else x
if c then x else x

examples.label: Ordered choice commits
examples.purpose: The Wrong first guess grammar with ordered choice: A's first match is final, so aab is rejected although it is in the language.

examples.label: Shortest alternative first
examples.purpose: With ordered choice A stops after one a and the rest never matches. Switch to complete search and it works; or reorder the alternatives.

examples.label: Longest alternative first
examples.purpose: The same language with the alternatives swapped: now ordered choice accepts it, because the long way is tried before the short one.

examples.label: Palindromes (ordered)
examples.purpose: Even palindromes such as aaaa are rejected: an inner S commits to its middle too early and is never asked again.
text: S -> a S a | b S b | a | b | eps

examples.label: Tiny statement language
examples.purpose: A small language written the way recursive-descent parsers are: a keyword picks the alternative. The tokens id and num stand for names and numbers.
text: Stmt -> id = Expr ; | print Expr ; | while ( Expr ) Block | if ( Expr ) Block Else
Expr' -> + Term Expr' | - Term Expr' | eps
strings: while ( id ) { print id ; id = id - num ; }
if ( id ) { id = num ; } else { id = num ; }

examples.label: Assignment or call
examples.purpose: Both statements start with id: the parser guesses assignment, backs up one token and tries the call. One more token of lookahead would avoid it.
strings: id = id + num ; id ( id , num ) ;

examples.label: Left recursion
examples.purpose: E calls E at the same position without reading anything, so a top-down parser would loop forever. The run stops at the first repeat.

examples.label: Hidden left recursion
examples.purpose: S -> A S looks right-recursive, but A can be empty, so S still calls itself before reading anything.

examples.label: Left recursion removed
examples.purpose: The usual expression grammar with the recursion moved to the right: the parser terminates and rarely has to undo anything.

examples.label: Repeated work
examples.purpose: Both alternatives of E start with T, so a T that is not followed by + is matched twice; every nesting level doubles the work.

examples.label: Repeated work, packrat
examples.purpose: The same grammar with a memo table: each nonterminal is parsed once per position, so the doubling at every nesting level is gone.
